title: How do you diffuse AI into the real world? — Varun Shenoy, Long Lake
talk_summary: A founder of a services-business rollup describes deploying agents into acquired property-management/HOA firms, arguing autonomy must be earned up a ladder (co-pilot → sync → async → long-running → co-worker) and that real-world traces from human-agent collaboration feed evals, post-training, and per-company customization. The core operational claim is that continual learning and user enablement are one loop, and that co-designing with the people doing the work is what makes adoption happen.

takeaways.what_they_do: Capture rich traces (tool calls, hiccups, papercuts) from agents doing real work, turn them into automatically-scored evals with ground truth, and promote weekly hill-climbing benchmarks into permanent regression tests.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every week our hill climbing benchmarks become a regression test. So, our agents get better and better over time.

takeaways.what_they_do: Compare AI-generated output against what a human ultimately submitted as a labeled signal, in addition to explicit thumbs up/down.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's a real diff between the data that the AI generated and what was ultimately submitted. That's rich information

takeaways.technique: Autonomy ladder, earn the right to async
takeaways.what_they_do: Deliberately stage agents from co-pilot to synchronous to asynchronous to long-running, only granting more autonomy once the task class is proven, rather than starting at full co-worker.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have to earn the right to do more. It's it's not enough to jump to the co-worker immediately

takeaways.what_they_do: Async agents are triggered by external events (task completion, job queue) rather than only by a user query, so they proactively pick up work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the user does not have to be the one that triggers them. You can have external triggers as well.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of waiting for models to be good at non-code knowledge work, encode that work as code so existing strong coding agents can execute it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what if we just use that code knowledge and represent knowledge work as code?

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat continual learning and user enablement as one loop: embed the product where people already work and observe real usage to drive improvements.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The agent only improves if people actually use it. And people only use the agent if it's worth adopting.
